raw_case_text:
In January 2001, a 32-year-old man referred to Montaserieh hospital of Mashhad, Iran, with a history of fevers and vomiting 10 days after returning from Pakistan. He also complained of dark urine and hematuria. He had no history of receiving prophylactic antimalarial drugs. He had previously been hospitalized in a small hospital with a diagnosis P. vivax infection and had received oral chloroquine therapy. Then the patient was referred to a specialized hospital in Mashhad city due to worsening symptoms. At admission, he had a temperature of 38.5 C and his other vital signs and consciousness level were normal. On physical examination, the patient had a tender abdomen and his spleen was palpable 5 cm below the left costal margin.
In laboratory studies, hemoglobin was 11.5 g/dL, hematocrit 34%, white blood cell count 16,000/mm3 , and platelet count was 45,000/mm 3 . His creatinine level was 1.9 mg/dL. Serum was assayed for total bilirubin (Bil), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), and alanine aminotransferase (ALT), using commercially available kits. The serum level of Bil was 2.3 mg/dL, LDH 1680 U/L (normal level: 80 - 100 U/L), AST 106 U/L, and ALT 29 U/L. Peripheral blood smear examination showed severe infection with P. falciparum and 75 to 85% of RBCs contained one to five parasites per cell (Figure 1). 
Patient probably had a mixed infection with P. vivax and P. falciparum that the P. vivax infection had been treated with oral chloroquine, but chloroquine-resistant P. falciparum remained and parasitemia had increased.
The patient was treated with intravenous quinine sulfate and oral primaquine. Then, he received primaquine (30 mg a day for 14 days) after the symptoms improvement for treating the probable mixed malaria infection. The improvement was considerable, so that parasitemia decreased by 40% after 24 hours and 1% after 4 days of posttreatment. During the treatment process, the patient developed dark urine and elevated creatine phosphokinase; thus, progression to acute renal failure was considered for him. Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) was exhibited in bilateral pulmonary infiltrates on the chest X-ray; also, he presented confusion due to cerebral malaria or superimposed a Gram-negative infection, so ceftriaxone was prescribed. However, patient was discharged after 10 days with no requirement for intubation, hemodialysis, or ICU admission. He had a good general condition at the last follow-up visit.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 32-year-old male presenting with high fever, vomiting, dark urine, hematuria, and left upper quadrant pain 10 days after returning from Pakistan.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed fevers, vomiting, dark urine, and hematuria 10 days after returning from travel to Pakistan. He was initially admitted to a local facility and treated with oral chloroquine, but experienced progressive clinical worsening prompting transfer to a specialized hospital. Following admission, he developed transient respiratory distress with bilateral lung infiltrates, acute renal impairment with elevated creatine kinase, and transient confusion, all managed medically.
subjective.past_medical_history: Travel to Pakistan 10 days prior to symptom onset; denied use of prophylactic antiparasitic therapy. Received oral chloroquine at an outside hospital prior to transfer.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, vomiting, dark urine, gross hematuria, and confusion. Medications: oral chloroquine at prior hospital. Allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature: 38.5 C; other baseline vital signs and consciousness initially normal. Abdomen: Generalized tenderness with prominent splenomegaly palpable 5 cm below the left costal margin. Subsequent hospital course: Developed confusion, tachypnea, and dark urine.
objective.routine_investigations: Hemoglobin: 11.5 g/dL, hematocrit: 34%, white blood cell count: 16,000/mm3, platelet count: 45,000/mm3. Serum creatinine: 1.9 mg/dL. Total serum bilirubin: 2.3 mg/dL, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH): 1,680 U/L (reference: 80-100 U/L), aspartate aminotransferase (AST): 106 U/L, alanine aminotransferase (ALT): 29 U/L. Serum creatine phosphokinase (CPK): Elevated. Urinalysis: Gross dark urine / hemoglobinuria. Chest X-ray: Bilateral pulmonary infiltrates consistent with acute lung injury / acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe, hyperparasitemic Plasmodium falciparum malaria (likely mixed infection with chloroquine-resistant P. falciparum following chloroquine treatment for P. vivax) complicated by acute renal impairment, hemoglobinuria/rhabdomyolysis, ARDS, and transient cerebral dysfunction.
Diagnostic confirmation: Peripheral blood smear demonstrated hyperparasitemic Plasmodium falciparum with 75% to 85% of erythrocytes containing 1 to 5 intraerythrocytic parasites per cell (parasitemia declined by 40% at 24 hours and to 1% at 4 days of therapy).
Plan & Outcome: Treated with intravenous quinine sulfate, followed by oral primaquine (30 mg daily for 14 days) for radical cure of suspected latent hypnozoites. Ceftriaxone was added empirically for acute confusion and pulmonary infiltrates. Managed supportively with hydration; renal impairment, ARDS, and confusion resolved without requiring mechanical ventilation, hemodialysis, or ICU transfer. Discharged in stable condition after 10 days.
